title: Adjacent Increasing Subarrays Detection II
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` of length `n`. Find the largest `k` such that `nums` contains two strictly increasing subarrays of length `k` that sit right next to each other: for some start index `a`, both `nums[a..a + k - 1]` and `nums[a + k..a + 2k - 1]` are strictly increasing, meaning every element is bigger than the one before it within each piece.

A subarray is a non-empty run of consecutive elements. Return that largest `k`. Since `n >= 2`, `k = 1` always works, so the answer is at least 1.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every `k` and every start directly costs O(n²) or more. Instead, cut `nums` into its maximal strictly increasing runs: a new run begins wherever `nums[i] <= nums[i - 1]`. Each of the two subarrays must fit inside a single run, so there are only two ways to place them:

- both inside one run of length `L`, giving up to `floor(L / 2)`;
- the first at the end of one run and the second at the start of the next, giving up to the shorter of the two lengths.

The run lengths come from a one-line DP: the run ending at `i` is one longer than the run ending at `i - 1` when `nums[i] > nums[i - 1]`, and 1 otherwise. Only the current and the previous run lengths are ever needed.

## Approach

1. `current` is the length of the run ending at index `i`, starting at 1 for `nums[0]` alone; `previous` is the length of the run before it, 0 at first.
2. For each `i` from 1: if `nums[i] > nums[i - 1]`, the run grows (`current += 1`). Otherwise the finished run becomes `previous` and a new run starts with `current = 1`.
3. Update `best` with `Math.floor(current / 2)` and `Math.min(previous, current)`. Checking at every `i` is harmless, because both candidates only grow while the run grows.
4. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`current` climbs to 5 over `[2, 5, 7, 8, 9]`, and `Math.floor(5 / 2)` makes `best = 2`. At `i = 5` the value 2 is not above 9, so `previous = 5` and `current = 1`. Over `[2, 3, 4]`, `current` reaches 3 and `Math.min(5, 3) = 3` sets `best = 3`: the pieces `[7, 8, 9]` and `[2, 3, 4]`. The values 3 and 1 each start a run of length 1, so the answer stays 3.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): a single pass.
- Space: O(1): two run lengths and `best`.

## Pitfalls

- Strictly increasing means equal neighbours end a run, as in example 2.
- Do not consider only run boundaries: in `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` both pieces sit in one run and the answer is 3.
- Binary search on `k` also works, because any valid `k` makes every smaller `k` valid too, but it costs an extra `log n` factor.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `current` | length of the strictly increasing run ending at `i` |
| `previous` | length of the run that ended just before the current one |
| `best` | the largest `k` found so far |
| `i` | the index being added to the scan |

narration.2: No run has finished yet, so the previous run has length 0.
narration.3: The run ending at index 0 is nums[0] by itself.
narration.4: best holds the largest k found so far.
narration.5: Add one index at a time from left to right.
narration.6: Is nums[i] strictly bigger than its left neighbour?
narration.7: Yes: the run ending at i is one longer than the run ending at i - 1.
narration.9: No: the run has ended, so remember its length...
narration.10: ...and start a new run holding only nums[i].
narration.12: Split the current run into two halves, or pair the end of the previous run with the start of this one.
narration.14: Return the largest k found anywhere.
